newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pakistan sees new IMF loan accord by end October.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sees new IMF loan accord by end October.

text.p: Pakistan Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz has predicted that the International Monetary Fund would agree to grant Islamabad a new line of credit to finance structural reforms before the end of October.

Aziz, speaking on Wednesday after a two-day World Bank conference on Pakistani development aid, said he was going to Washington on Thursday for new talks with IMF officials on a new so-called Extended Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) to support structural reforms.
A previous $1.2 billion ESAF was derailed when the IMF concluded that a previous caretaker government could not meet its conditions.
Aziz told reporters he could not say how big the new ESAF would be. That would be set by the IMF after the government completed its new budget plan, expected in June, he said.
Aziz led a team of eight Pakistani officials in Paris to outline government reform plans to 14 donor nations and 11 international aid organisations at the World Bank's European headquarters.
The minister said at the close of the two-day meeting that he was "very pleased" by donors' response to the plans.

The economic reform package was unveiled by the government of Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on March 28, shortly after the IMF withdrew its previous line of credit. Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League was swept to power in February 3 elections.
The government has asked for fresh commitments of $2.268 billion from the donor group for 1997-98, but donors made no formal pledges at the meeting, Pakistani and World Bank officials said.
"This was a non-pledging development meeting," said one Pakistani official.
"The cycle of commitment is now well established," added Aziz, predicting donors eventually would pledge more than the government had asked for.
A World Bank official agreed that the Pakistani team's reform programme had been "broadly endorsed" by the donors.
Aziz said the key goal of the government reform package was "to revive the economy".

He said Islamabad hoped for a major stimulus from plans to broaden the tax base, go after tax cheats and smugglers, reduce tariffs, encourage farm production, slim down the government, promote trade and foreign investment and spur social progress.
"There was almost unanimous consensus in the meeting that these were the kinds of reforms that should have taken place some time ago," Aziz said.
Hafiz Pasha, deputy chairman of Pakistan's planning commission predicted that 1996-97 economic growth would be about 4.5 percent with inflation at 12 percent to 13 percent for the current year.
